purpose: Rosiglitazone is used to help control blood sugar levels in adults with type 2 diabetes. It is used along with diet and exercise, and sometimes with other diabetes medicines. It helps your body use insulin more effectively so your blood sugar stays in a healthier range.
how_it_works: Your body has special receptors in fat and muscle cells that help control how your body responds to insulin. Rosiglitazone works by activating these receptors, which makes your cells more sensitive to insulin. Think of it like oiling a rusty lock — it helps insulin 'unlock' your cells so sugar can get inside and be used for energy instead of building up in your blood.
common_side_effects: Weight gain is one of the most common side effects. You may also notice fluid retention or mild swelling, especially in your hands, ankles, or feet. Some people experience mild upper respiratory infections, headaches, or back pain. Tell your doctor if swelling becomes significant.
warnings: Rosiglitazone can increase the risk of heart failure, especially if you already have heart problems — contact your doctor right away if you notice sudden weight gain, shortness of breath, or severe swelling. It may also slightly increase the risk of bone fractures, particularly in women. Because of heart-related concerns, this medication is only available through a special restricted access program in the US. Do not use it if you have active liver problems. It can also cause or worsen macular edema (a type of eye swelling), so tell your eye doctor you take this medicine.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose is 4 mg once a day or split into 2 mg twice a day. Your doctor may increase it to 8 mg per day if needed after about 8 to 12 weeks. It can be taken with or without food. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions for your dose.
